title: Article 14: discrimination and its parasitic nature
subtitle: Ambit, status, and the four-stage test that carries every Article 14 claim
objectives: Explain why Article 14 is 'parasitic' — it cannot be breached on its own, only in conjunction with the ambit of another Convention right — and identify what 'ambit' requires

Apply the four-stage discrimination test (ambit, analogous situation, other status, justification) to a new fact pattern, including the Thlimmenos principle that discrimination can arise from a failure to treat differently-situated people differently

Explain how courts vary the intensity of the justification stage depending on subject matter, contrasting the Belmarsh case's rejection of the government's justification with R (DA) v SSWP's deference in welfare policy, and state how s3 HRA was used in Ghaidan to avoid a finding of discrimination

leadingAuthorities.citation: A v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2004] UKHL 56 (the Belmarsh case)
leadingAuthorities.role: Indefinite detention of foreign terrorism suspects discriminated on grounds of nationality/immigration status; justification rejected
Uses s3 HRA to read 'spouse' succession rights to include same-sex partners, avoiding an Article 14/8 breach
Establishes that Article 14 can be breached by treating relevantly different situations the same, without objective justification

leadingAuthorities.citation: R (DA) v Secretary of State for Work and Pensions [2019] UKSC 21
leadingAuthorities.role: Illustrates wide deference to the state's justification in socio-economic/welfare policy despite disparate impact

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Article 14 is the article students most often either skip entirely or bolt on as an afterthought — 'and this is also discriminatory' — without running any of its structure. It has almost no independent content; everything it protects depends on doing four specific steps correctly, in order. This lesson is built around that structure, because the structure is the mark scheme.

profileHooks.weakApplication: You know the four stages by name. The test pool here leans heavily on spotting which stage a given fact actually fails at — expect scenarios engineered to trip on 'ambit' or 'other status', not just the obvious ones.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and Part 2 and be able to state all four stages of the test unprompted before moving on. Nothing later in this lesson makes sense without that scaffold in place first.

overview.hook: Article 14 is the only Convention right in this module that cannot stand on its own two feet. It has no independent existence — no fact pattern is ever 'just' an Article 14 problem — and yet it does more real work in practice than almost any other article, because it is the route by which the same interference with the same right can be lawful for one group and unlawful for another. This lesson builds the machinery from the ground up: four stages, applied in order, every time.

parts.heading: A right with no independent existence
parts.voice: structural — states the counter-intuitive framing before the doctrine that explains it
body: Article 14 reads, in essence: the enjoyment of the rights and freedoms set out in the Convention shall be secured without discrimination on any ground such as sex, race, colour, language, religion, political or other opinion, national or social origin, association with a national minority, property, birth or other status. Read it carefully and notice what it does not say. It does not say 'no one shall be discriminated against.' It says the enjoyment of Convention rights shall be secured without discrimination. Article 14 has no free-standing content of its own — it is, in the standard phrase, parasitic: it can only be breached in conjunction with another Convention right, never alone.

That does not mean the other right also has to be breached. This is the detail students most often get backwards. A claimant does not need to show that, say, Article 8 was itself violated — only that the facts fall within the ambit (sometimes called the 'scope') of Article 8, meaning the subject matter is one Article 8 touches, even if the state's conduct on those facts would otherwise be perfectly lawful under Article 8 read alone. Ambit is a deliberately generous, low threshold — it exists to let Article 14 do its real job, which is catching unequal treatment in how a state exercises powers that are themselves lawful.

A v Secretary of State for the Home Department — the Belmarsh case — is the case to anchor this in. Following the 2001 attacks, Part 4 of the Anti-terrorism, Crime and Security Act 2001 allowed indefinite detention without trial of foreign nationals suspected of involvement in terrorism, where they could not be deported because of Article 3 risk in their home country. UK nationals suspected of exactly the same conduct could not be detained under the scheme at all — only deported UK nationals cannot be. The scheme plainly fell within the ambit of Article 5 (liberty), since it authorised detention; the question Article 14 then asked was whether distinguishing foreign nationals from UK nationals, for identical suspected conduct, was discrimination on a status ground, and if so, whether it was justified.

components.definition: Article 14 cannot be breached on its own — a claim must fall within the 'ambit' of another Convention right, meaning the subject matter is one that right touches, even where that other right is not itself violated on the facts.

interaction.prompt: To succeed on an Article 14 claim, must the claimant also show that the other Convention right relied on (e.g. Article 8) was itself violated?
options: No — only that the facts fall within the ambit of that other right
Yes — Article 14 only applies once the other right has already been breached
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. This is the single most important structural feature of Article 14: 'ambit' is a much lower bar than 'violation'. A state can act entirely lawfully under Article 8 and still discriminate, within Article 8's ambit, in breach of Article 14.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Reconsider what 'ambit' means. If Article 14 required the other right to be violated too, it would add almost nothing — its whole function is to catch discrimination in how a state exercises powers that are, considered alone, lawful. Ambit, not violation, is the threshold.

parts.heading: The four-stage test
parts.voice: reference — a structural checklist students will return to before every Article 14 answer
body: Every Article 14 problem, however different the facts look, is answered by working through the same four stages in the same order. Learn them as a sequence, not a list, because a claim that fails at an early stage never reaches the later ones — and knowing which stage a fact pattern actually fails at is most of what separates a strong answer from a weak one.

Stage one: does the treatment complained of fall within the ambit of another substantive Convention right? Stage two: is there a difference in treatment between the claimant and another person (real or hypothetical) in an analogous, or relevantly similar, situation? Stage three: is that difference in treatment on the ground of a status listed in Article 14, or an 'other status' — a category the Strasbourg and domestic courts read broadly, extending well beyond the listed grounds to cover things like sexual orientation, immigration status, or disability. Stage four: is the difference in treatment objectively justified — does it pursue a legitimate aim, and is it proportionate to that aim?

One refinement belongs here before you move on, because it inverts stage two in a way students often miss entirely: Thlimmenos v Greece establishes that Article 14 discrimination can arise not only from treating similarly-situated people differently, but from treating differently-situated people the same, without objective justification for the failure to differentiate. Keep that in mind through the rest of this lesson — 'discrimination' in Article 14's sense is broader than the everyday meaning of the word.

components.label: The four-stage Article 14 test
points: 1. Ambit — do the facts fall within the scope of another substantive Convention right?
2. Analogous situation — is the claimant treated differently from someone in a relevantly similar situation (or, per Thlimmenos, the same as someone in a relevantly different situation)?
3. Status — is the difference in treatment on a listed ground or an 'other status', read broadly?
4. Justification — does the difference in treatment pursue a legitimate aim, proportionately?

interaction.prompt: Put the four stages of the Article 14 test in the order a court applies them.
items: Ask whether the facts fall within the ambit of another Convention right
Ask whether the claimant is treated differently from a person in an analogous situation (or the same as a person in a relevantly different one)
Ask whether the difference in treatment is on a listed or 'other' status ground
Ask whether the difference in treatment is objectively and proportionately justified
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the sequence. Each stage gates the next — a claim that fails 'ambit' never needs a justification analysis at all, because there is nothing yet for Article 14 to bite on.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Check the order again. Ambit comes first because without it Article 14 has no foothold at all; justification comes last because it only needs answering once a difference in treatment, on a status ground, has already been established.

parts.heading: Thlimmenos: discrimination by refusing to differentiate
parts.voice: case-narrative — tells the story before naming the principle it generates
body: Iakovos Thlimmenos was a Jehovah's Witness who, on religious grounds, refused to wear a military uniform during compulsory service and was convicted of insubordination. Some years later, he applied to become a chartered accountant. Greek law barred anyone with a serious criminal conviction from the profession — a blanket rule, applied without any exception for the circumstances of the conviction. Thlimmenos was refused registration solely because of his insubordination conviction, on exactly the same basis as someone convicted of, say, fraud or violence.

The European Court of Human Rights held that Greece had violated Article 14 read with Article 9 — not because Thlimmenos was treated worse than other people with criminal convictions (he was treated identically to them), but precisely because he was treated identically to them. His conviction arose from a conscientious, religiously-motivated refusal, a fundamentally different kind of conduct from the dishonesty or violence the professional bar was designed to screen out, and Greece had offered no objective justification for refusing to draw that distinction.

This is the principle now known simply as Thlimmenos: Article 14 is breached where a state, without objective and reasonable justification, fails to treat differently persons whose situations are significantly different. It matters because it doubles the range of facts Article 14 can catch — not only 'why was I singled out' claims, but 'why wasn't my different situation recognised' claims, which come up constantly in benefits, immigration and regulatory contexts where a single rule is applied uniformly to people whose circumstances plainly are not uniform.

components.factsShort: A Jehovah's Witness convicted of insubordination for refusing, on religious grounds, to wear a military uniform was later barred from becoming a chartered accountant under a blanket rule excluding anyone with a serious criminal conviction.
components.ratioShort: Article 14 is breached where a state, without objective justification, fails to treat differently persons whose situations are relevantly and significantly different, not only where it treats similar people differently.

expanded.facts: Greek professional regulation excluded anyone convicted of a felony from becoming a chartered accountant, with no distinction drawn between the nature or circumstances of different convictions. Thlimmenos's conviction arose from a single act of religiously-motivated conscientious objection, not from dishonesty or any conduct bearing on fitness for the accountancy profession.
expanded.judgmentExtract: The Court held that the right not to be discriminated against in the enjoyment of Convention rights is also violated when states, without an objective and reasonable justification, fail to treat differently persons whose situations are significantly different. Applying a uniform bar to Thlimmenos, without any mechanism to consider whether his particular conviction was relevant to fitness to practise, amounted to unjustified discrimination on grounds of religion, engaging Article 9.
expanded.significance: Thlimmenos is the leading authority for 'indirect' or 'failure to differentiate' discrimination under Article 14 — it is cited whenever a uniform rule, applied without any capacity to account for a claimant's materially different circumstances, produces an unjustified disparate impact.

interaction.prompt: Tap the fact that makes this a Thlimmenos-style claim, rather than an ordinary 'treated worse than others' discrimination claim.
interaction.scenarioText: A local authority applies a blanket policy refusing housing priority to anyone with a gap in their tenancy history, without any exception. Maya, a survivor of domestic abuse, fled her previous tenancy abruptly for safety reasons and has a six-month gap as a result. She is refused priority on exactly the same basis as an applicant who simply abandoned a tenancy to avoid rent arrears.
tappableSpans: fled her previous tenancy abruptly for safety reasons
refused priority on exactly the same basis
interaction.correctSpan: refused priority on exactly the same basis
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the Thlimmenos move: Maya isn't complaining she was singled out for worse treatment — she's complaining that a materially different situation (fleeing abuse) was collapsed into the same category as an unrelated one (rent-arrears abandonment), without any justification for refusing to distinguish them.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look for the fact showing Maya was treated identically to someone in a relevantly different situation, not differently from someone similar. Thlimmenos claims turn on a state's refusal to draw a distinction it should have drawn.

parts.heading: Justification: how much deference does the state get?
parts.voice: argumentative — contrasts two outcomes to expose the variable it turns on
body: Stage four is where most Article 14 claims are actually won or lost, and it is also the stage where the intensity of review varies most sharply depending on subject matter. Belmarsh shows what happens when the state loses. The House of Lords accepted the government's stated aim — protecting national security from a terrorist threat — was legitimate, but held the scheme was not rationally connected to that aim in a non-discriminatory way: if UK nationals posed the same suspected risk, detaining only foreign nationals did nothing to address the threat from UK nationals, while doing nothing to explain why nationality, rather than actual dangerousness, was the line drawn. Lord Bingham's leading speech held the measure was disproportionate and discriminatory, and the House made a declaration of incompatibility.

R (DA) v Secretary of State for Work and Pensions shows the opposite result, in a very different policy area. Lone parents challenged the household benefit cap, arguing it discriminated against them — particularly those with children under two, for whom the state does not require work-related activity — because it removed an equivalent amount of income regardless of whether reducing household size or increasing paid work was realistically possible for that group. The Supreme Court, by a majority, held that even accepting the disparate impact, the justification stage was satisfied: welfare and economic policy is an area where courts extend a wide margin of discretion to the executive and legislature, and a policy will not be found unjustified merely because it could have been designed more generously, provided it is not 'manifestly without reasonable foundation'.

Put side by side, Belmarsh and DA are not inconsistent — they show the same four-stage test producing different outcomes because courts calibrate how hard they scrutinise 'justification' to the subject matter: national security detention of a class of persons attracts close scrutiny, especially where the safeguard against arbitrary detention (Article 5) is engaged; broad economic and welfare policy attracts a lighter touch, described as asking only whether the choice is manifestly without reasonable foundation, not whether it was the best or fairest choice available.

components.title: How much scrutiny does the justification stage get?
components.description: A rough guide to where a subject area sits on the deference spectrum for Article 14's justification stage.

nodes.label: What kind of interest is the state advancing?
Liberty, physical security, core status distinctions (e.g. nationality-based detention)
Close scrutiny — courts require a tight, evidenced connection between means and aim (Belmarsh)
Broad economic, welfare or fiscal policy
Light-touch review — 'manifestly without reasonable foundation' standard (R (DA))

components.textAlternative: Where the state's justification concerns liberty and security, or draws a distinction on a core status such as nationality, courts apply close scrutiny and require a tightly evidenced connection between the measure and its aim, as in Belmarsh. Where the justification concerns broad economic, welfare or fiscal policy, courts apply a much lighter touch, asking only whether the choice is manifestly without reasonable foundation, as in R (DA) v SSWP.

interaction.prompt: Why did R (DA) v SSWP reach a different result on justification from A v SSHD (Belmarsh), despite both involving accepted disparate impact on a status group?
options: Because the benefit cap did not actually cause any disparate impact on lone parents, unlike Belmarsh's detention scheme

Because courts apply markedly less intense scrutiny to broad economic and welfare policy than to measures affecting liberty and security, and will not strike down a welfare measure unless it is manifestly without reasonable foundation
Because Article 14 does not apply to welfare benefits at all, so the claim in DA failed at the ambit stage
interaction.trapExplanation: The Court in DA accepted the disparate impact was real, so the first option misstates the case, and the claim in DA passed the ambit and status stages without difficulty, so the third option is also wrong. The actual explanation is that the intensity of review at the justification stage itself varies by subject matter — the same four-stage test, applied with very different levels of deference.

parts.heading: When Article 14 wins without a declaration: Ghaidan and section 3
parts.voice: Socratic — poses the remedial puzzle before resolving it with Ghaidan
body: Here's a question worth sitting with before the answer: if a court finds legislation does discriminate in a way Article 14 forbids, does it have to declare that legislation incompatible and leave Parliament to fix it — or can the court itself fix the discrimination by reading the statute differently? Ghaidan v Godin-Mendoza answers this, and answers it dramatically.

The Rent Act 1977 allowed a person who had been living with a deceased tenant 'as his or her wife or husband' to succeed to the tenancy on the same protected terms. Mr Godin-Mendoza had lived with his same-sex partner, the original tenant, for years in a long-term, committed relationship, and sought to succeed to the tenancy on that basis when his partner died. Read literally, the phrase 'as his or her wife or husband' referred only to heterosexual couples living together as if married — a distinction on grounds of sexual orientation, within the ambit of Article 8 (respect for the home), and precisely the kind of Article 14 problem this lesson has been building towards.

The House of Lords held that Parliament could not have intended this distinction to survive the Human Rights Act, and used section 3 HRA — the strong interpretive obligation to read legislation compatibly with Convention rights 'so far as it is possible to do so' — to read the phrase as extending to a same-sex partner living together 'as if they were his wife or husband'. This was, by the majority's own admission, a bold use of section 3: it changed the practical meaning of the provision, going, as Lord Nicholls put it, against the grain of the language Parliament actually used, while stopping short of what the majority regarded as illegitimate judicial legislation. Contrast this with Bellinger v Bellinger, decided the same year, where the House concluded a compatible reading of 'marriage' to include a person's acquired gender was not possible under section 3 at all, and issued a declaration of incompatibility instead. Ghaidan is the clearest illustration that where a discriminatory reading can be avoided through interpretation, courts will reach for section 3 first — a declaration under section 4 is the fallback, not the first resort.

components.factsShort: The Rent Act 1977 allowed a person living with a deceased tenant 'as his or her wife or husband' to succeed to the tenancy; the surviving same-sex partner of a tenant sought the same succession right.
components.ratioShort: Section 3 HRA required 'as his or her wife or husband' to be read as including a same-sex partner living together as if they were spouses, to avoid an Article 14/Article 8 breach — even though this went against the grain of the statutory language.

expanded.facts: Mr Godin-Mendoza had lived with the deceased statutory tenant, his same-sex partner, in a long, stable relationship. On a literal reading, the Rent Act's succession provision for a person living 'as his or her wife or husband' extended only to opposite-sex cohabitants.
expanded.judgmentExtract: The majority held that the discriminatory effect of a literal reading, on grounds of sexual orientation, fell within the ambit of Article 8 and breached Article 14 without justification. Section 3 HRA required the phrase to be interpreted, if at all possible, compatibly with Convention rights; the majority held this was possible here, reading the provision to extend to a survivor of a same-sex couple living together as if they were a married or civil-partnered couple, notwithstanding that this changed the ordinary meaning of 'wife or husband'.
expanded.significance: Ghaidan is the leading illustration of how far section 3 HRA can stretch statutory language, and of the practical hierarchy between sections 3 and 4: interpretation first, wherever linguistically possible, with a declaration of incompatibility only where — as in the same year's Bellinger v Bellinger — no compatible reading can be achieved without effectively rewriting the statute.

interaction.prompt: A workplace pension scheme's rules provide a survivor's pension to an employee's 'widow or widower' on the employee's death. Priya, in a long-term same-sex civil partnership with the employee, is refused the survivor's pension on the basis she is neither a widow nor a widower in the literal sense. Analyse whether Article 14 is engaged and how a court might resolve the interpretive question, applying Ghaidan.
factsToOrder: The scheme's rules use gendered marital language ('widow or widower')
Priya was in a long-term civil partnership with the deceased employee
She is refused the pension on a literal reading of the rules
The pension scheme is a private arrangement given effect through legislation engaging Article 1 Protocol 1/Article 8
Parliament's evident purpose was to protect long-term partners of employees, not to draw a distinction by sexual orientation

scaffolds.support: Full model IRAC answer shown, with each fact mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, drags facts into Application, writes Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether refusing Priya a survivor's pension under gendered marital language breaches Article 14, and if so, whether the court can resolve this through interpretation rather than a declaration of incompatibility.
modelAnswer.rule: Article 14 is engaged where a difference in treatment on a status ground (sexual orientation) falls within the ambit of another right and is unjustified. Where legislation can be read compatibly 'so far as possible', section 3 HRA requires that reading in preference to a declaration of incompatibility under section 4, per Ghaidan — even where this departs from the literal wording, provided it does not contradict the underlying legislative scheme.
modelAnswer.application: A literal reading of 'widow or widower' excludes a same-sex civil partner solely on grounds of sexual orientation, within the ambit of the property/family-life interests the pension protects — the same structure as Ghaidan. As in Ghaidan, the evident underlying purpose is to protect long-term partners, not to distinguish by sexual orientation, so reading 'widow or widower' to include a civil partner is consistent with, not contrary to, the scheme's own object.
modelAnswer.conclusion: Following Ghaidan, a court is likely to use section 3 to read the pension rule as extending to Priya as a civil partner, avoiding an Article 14/Article 8 breach without needing a declaration of incompatibility.

testPool.prompt: What does it mean to say Article 14 is a 'parasitic' right?
acceptableAnswers: it cannot be breached alone, only within the ambit of another Convention right
it has no free-standing existence and must attach to another right's ambit
testPool.modelAnswer: Article 14 has no independent content of its own — a claim can only succeed if the facts fall within the ambit of another substantive Convention right; it cannot be breached in isolation.

testPool.prompt: Is the list of grounds in Article 14 ('sex, race, colour... or other status') a closed list?
options: No — 'other status' is read broadly and the list is illustrative, not exhaustive
Yes — only the listed grounds can ever found an Article 14 claim

testPool.prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of the four stages of the Article 14 test?
options: Ambit of another Convention right
Analogous situation (or Thlimmenos failure to differentiate)
Status ground
Exhaustion of domestic remedies
testPool.trapExplanation: Exhaustion of domestic remedies is a Strasbourg admissibility requirement for bringing a case to the European Court of Human Rights — it has nothing to do with the substantive four-stage Article 14 test applied by a domestic or Strasbourg court once a case is properly before it.

testPool.prompt: Article 14 lists 'sex, race, colour, language, religion, political or other opinion, national or social origin, association with a national minority, property, birth or other status.' What is the function of the words 'or other status' at the end of this list?
options: They restrict the list to only the most analogous unlisted grounds, such as language variants
They open the list to further grounds not expressly named, which courts have read to include sexual orientation, immigration status and disability
They have no independent legal effect and simply restate the preceding list
testPool.explanation: 'Other status' is the textual hook that lets Article 14 keep pace with grounds the drafters did not name in 1950 — sexual orientation (as in Ghaidan) and immigration/nationality status (as in Belmarsh) are both established as 'other status' grounds through case law.

testPool.prompt: A claimant alleges an immigration policy discriminates on grounds of national origin, engaging Article 8. Put the court's reasoning steps in order.
items: Confirm the policy falls within the ambit of Article 8
Identify a comparator in an analogous situation treated differently (or a failure to differentiate)
Confirm national origin is a status ground under Article 14
Assess whether the difference in treatment is objectively and proportionately justified

testPool.prompt: In the passage below adapted from A v SSHD (Belmarsh), highlight the sentence stating the core discrimination finding.
testPool.passage: The threat the government identified was a threat from international terrorism generally, not a threat confined to foreign nationals. The scheme detained only foreign nationals suspected of exactly the conduct that, if committed by a UK national, would not lead to detention at all. A power of indefinite detention exercised only against one group, where the underlying suspected conduct and threat is common to both groups, is a difference in treatment on the ground of nationality that has not been shown to be justified. The appropriate remedy is a declaration of incompatibility.
testPool.ratioSentence: A power of indefinite detention exercised only against one group, where the underlying suspected conduct and threat is common to both groups, is a difference in treatment on the ground of nationality that has not been shown to be justified.

testPool.prompt: Which scenario is more likely to satisfy the 'ambit' stage of Article 14?
testPool.scenarioA: A local authority's housing allocation scheme gives lower priority to applicants from outside the borough, affecting where and whether they can access settled accommodation.
testPool.scenarioB: A local authority publishes a public information leaflet in only one language, and a resident complains this is generally unfair, without identifying any Convention right the leaflet touches.
testPool.explanation: A engages Article 8 (home/private life) through its direct effect on access to accommodation, giving Article 14 a foothold. B identifies no Convention right the facts touch at all — 'generally unfair' is not enough; Article 14 needs a specific right's ambit to attach to.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact that makes this a Thlimmenos-style claim.
testPool.scenarioText: A prison's standard disciplinary process treats a rule-breach caused by a diagnosed cognitive impairment identically to a rule-breach caused by deliberate defiance, applying the same sanction in both cases without any mechanism to consider the difference.
tappableSpans: the same sanction in both cases
without any mechanism to consider the difference
testPool.correctSpan: without any mechanism to consider the difference
testPool.explanation: Thlimmenos claims turn on the absence of any capacity to differentiate between relevantly different situations, not merely on the existence of different underlying causes. The rule itself might be fine in most cases; the problem is its rigidity in the face of a materially different situation.

testPool.prompt: A state pension top-up scheme is available only to claimants who have been continuously resident for ten years, with no exception for those who left temporarily for reasons beyond their control (e.g. fleeing a humanitarian crisis abroad while a UK national). Which stage of the Article 14 test does this fact pattern most obviously engage first?
options: Ambit — residence-based welfare entitlement is likely to fall within the ambit of Article 1 Protocol 1 (possessions) or, depending on the scheme, Article 8
Justification — the scheme is automatically unjustified because it has exceptions missing
Status — residence length is never capable of being an 'other status'
testPool.explanation: Before asking about justification or status, the test starts with ambit. A welfare/pension entitlement scheme typically falls within A1P1's protection of possessions (or Article 8, depending on the facts), giving Article 14 its foothold before the later stages are even reached.

testPool.prompt: How confident are you that R (DA) v SSWP found the benefit cap's disparate impact on lone parents with young children to be an unjustified breach of Article 14?
testPool.explanation: The Supreme Court majority accepted the disparate impact but held it was not manifestly without reasonable foundation, applying the wide margin of deference courts give to welfare and economic policy — so no Article 14 breach was found.

testPool.prompt: A local authority's bereavement support policy defines 'immediate family' eligible for a support grant as 'spouse, civil partner, or blood relative'. Jamie, who had lived with his long-term unmarried partner for fifteen years and jointly raised her children, is refused the grant on her death because he is neither a spouse, civil partner, nor blood relative. Analyse whether s3 HRA, applying Ghaidan, could be used to extend the definition to Jamie.
factsToOrder: Jamie lived with his partner for fifteen years in a marriage-like relationship
The scheme's wording is limited to spouse, civil partner or blood relative
The grant scheme is delegated legislation engaging Article 8 (private/family life)
The evident purpose is to support those in the deceased's closest personal relationships
Extending the definition to long-term unmarried partners would not contradict that underlying purpose

scaffolds.support: Full model IRAC answer shown, with each fact mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, drags facts into Application, writes Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether the exclusion of long-term unmarried partners from the bereavement grant breaches Article 14 read with Article 8, and whether section 3 HRA can cure this through interpretation.
modelAnswer.rule: Article 14 requires a difference in treatment on a status ground (marital/relationship status) within the ambit of another right to be justified; where it is not, section 3 HRA requires legislation to be read compatibly so far as possible, per Ghaidan, provided the reading does not contradict the underlying legislative scheme.
modelAnswer.application: The grant scheme falls within Article 8's ambit (family and private life support), and excluding long-term unmarried partners while including spouses and civil partners is a difference in treatment on relationship-status grounds that would need justification. As in Ghaidan, the underlying purpose — supporting those in the deceased's closest relationships — is not contradicted by extending the definition to include a long-term, marriage-like partnership; the exclusion looks like an oversight in drafting rather than a deliberate policy choice.
modelAnswer.conclusion: Following Ghaidan, a court is likely to read 'immediate family' to extend to a long-term partner such as Jamie, avoiding an unjustified Article 14/Article 8 breach without needing a declaration of incompatibility.

testPool.prompt: A government minister argues a discriminatory measure is justified simply because Parliament debated and approved it. Applying Belmarsh and R (DA), is parliamentary approval alone sufficient justification under Article 14's fourth stage?
options: Yes — once Parliament has approved a measure, courts cannot revisit its justification at all
No — parliamentary approval may be relevant context, but the court must still independently assess legitimate aim and proportionality, with the intensity of that assessment varying by subject matter
No — parliamentary approval is actually evidence the measure is unjustified
testPool.trapExplanation: The first option describes a form of near-total deference the courts in both Belmarsh and DA explicitly rejected — Belmarsh struck down primary legislation's discriminatory effect despite parliamentary approval. The third overstates the opposite way — approval is neutral, not evidence of unjustifiability. The real position is a variable-intensity independent assessment, illustrated by the contrast between Belmarsh's close scrutiny and DA's light touch.

testPool.prompt: A uniform school attendance policy applies identical sanctions to a persistent truant and to a child whose absences are entirely caused by a disability requiring frequent hospital treatment, without any capacity to distinguish the two. Is this capable of being an Article 14 problem?
options: Yes — this is a Thlimmenos-type claim: relevantly different situations treated identically without justification
No — Article 14 only ever concerns treating similar people differently, never treating different people the same

testPool.prompt: Name the case establishing that Article 14 can be breached by failing to treat differently-situated people differently, without objective justification.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The single most common mistake in this lesson's test items is skipping straight to 'justification' without first establishing ambit, an analogous (or Thlimmenos) comparator, and a status ground. If a claim fails at stage one, there is nothing left to justify — check the earlier stages before writing anything about proportionality.
